html:
De Administrando Imperio, "On governing the empire", is a handbook that the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII put together around 948 to 952 for his son and heir, Romanos II. Its Greek title is simply "To my own son Romanos"; the Latin name came from a later editor.

It advises how to deal with the peoples around the empire: whom to play off against whom, what gifts to send, which demands to refuse. Among its topics:

  • the Pechenegs of the steppe, as allies to hold the Rus', Magyars and Bulgars in check
  • the Rus' and their yearly voyage down the Dnieper, with the Norse and Slavic names of its rapids
  • the Khazars, the Magyars and the peoples of the Caucasus
  • the origins of the Croats and Serbs, and the cities of Dalmatia
  • the early history of Venice and of the Arabs

It was meant for the emperor alone. Today it is a main source on the early history of the Rus', Croats, Serbs and Hungarians, and its story of how the Croats and Serbs came to the Balkans is still argued over.
